newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan forex reform brings opportunity, competition.
newsitem.headline: Japan forex reform brings opportunity, competition.

text.p: The first drastic reform of Japan's foreign exchange controls in 17 years is expected to pry open new business opportunities while increasing competition, experts and industry sources say.
"We may have coffee shops where customers can pay in dollars. Travellers from around the world may be able to use dollars to shop in Japan," a Finance Ministry official said.
Japan's Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law currently limits the lucrative foreign exchange business to licensed institutions, resulting in high commissions.
"Due to a lack of competition, the current situation may be somewhat disadvantageous for bank customers," the ministry official said.
About 12,000 institutions, including regional branches of authorised banks, some hotels and travel agencies, are licensed to exchange foreign currencies, he said.

In March the cabinet of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto submitted a foreign exchange reform bill to parliament that would allow any retail store, supermarket or individual to exchange foreign currencies without official authorisation.
The bill, devised as a front-runner of Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms, is expected to pass during the current session of parliament and to take effect in April 1998.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday that the reforms would help create a variety of financial services that would be useful for both individuals and corporate investors in Japan.
Retail stores and airline companies are among those that have expressed interest in entering the foreign exchange arena.

"If there is demand from our customers, we will start considering the possibility of exchanging currencies at our stores," said a spokesman for Ito-Yokado Co Ltd, one of Japan's leading supermarket operators.

"It (the law's revision) will increase the potential for new business in general, regardless of whether or not we get involved in such operations," said a spokeswoman at Daiei Inc, Japan's largest retail chain operator.
Kousei Yamada, assistant manager of public relations at Japan Airlines Co Ltd, said his company is mulling whether to offer foreign exchange services at its airport counters.
"We are calling for a review of the topic. First, we need to study if there is any need for such operations," he said.
Exchange rates for individual customers are currently set freely every day at licenced commercial banks.

An informal survey of major city banks in Japan found that individuals buying dollars for yen were charged a commission of 1.80 to 3.00 yen per dollar, which is added to the bank's fixed exchange rate.
Banks charged commissions of 3.00 to 3.75 yen for German marks, 7.70 to 10.00 yen for Australian dollars and 8.00 to 13.00 yen for British pounds.
The ministry official said that, although reform would boost competition among businesses offering foreign exchange services, newcomers would need professional skills to succeed.

"To enter the foreign exchange business you need to have specialised knowledge. A convenience store, for instance, needs to understand foreign exchange risk in order to conduct such business," he said.
